summary: Alberta voted by about 76% to stay in Canada in Monday's referendum, and September inflation rose to 3.1%, a bit below forecasts, ahead of the Bank of Canada's Oct. 28 rate decision.
body: Early results from Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum show about 76% of voters chose to remain in Canada on Question 10, while about 24% backed a second, binding vote on leaving[^1][^2]. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans "chose unity", and Premier Danielle Smith, who said she voted to stay, plans a televised address Tuesday night[^2]. The other nine questions, on immigration and the Constitution, are still being counted, with results expected by Wednesday[^1]. Smith needs yes votes on those to claim a mandate to bargain with Ottawa; Carney urged a no[^1].

Statistics Canada said prices rose 3.1% over the year to September, up from 3.0% in August[^3]. Gasoline was the main driver, up 27.8%; without gas, inflation was 2.2%[^3]. Grocery prices rose 1.7%, the smallest yearly gain since May 2024, and university tuition rose 2.4% nationally and 2.1% in Ontario after the province ended its tuition freeze[^3]. Ontario's overall rate, 2.5%, was the lowest of any province[^5][^4]. Economists had expected 3.2%[^4].

The Bank of Canada sets its key interest rate (which shapes loan and mortgage costs) on Oct. 28[^4]. Federal officials say 50 investigators, led by the military police's National Investigation Service with RCMP support, are looking into the Oct. 17 fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta that killed four soldiers and injured 39 people[^7][^6]. The cause has not been determined, and the Armed Forces say there is no sign of terrorism[^6]. Otherwise, there was no major Canada-US tariff or Ontario news in this window.
differences: Separatist organizer Jeff Rath said "we're not going anywhere", while pro-Canada campaigners said separatists should accept they are not the majority[^2]. Smith has said she expects people to "accept it and move on"[^1]. On rates, Governor Tiff Macklem said the bank is ready to raise rates if energy prices spread to other prices. BMO's Douglas Porter said the inflation report does not strengthen the case for a hike. My read: these views are not far apart, because both depend on whether the gas-price jump spreads[^4].
